The radial primitive is \(\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\). At the upper limit, \(\sqrt{a^2+a^2\cos2\theta}=a\sqrt2\cos\theta\), because cos θ>0 on this interval.

question_paragraphs: The source asks to show ∬r²sinθ drdθ=2a²/3 over “the semi circle r=2a sinθ and above the initial line”.
paragraphs: Source issue: the source calls \(r=2a\sin\theta\) a “semi circle” and asks for \(2a^2/3\). For a>0 the polar equation is the full circle \(x^2+(y-a)^2=a^2\), already wholly above the initial line. A separate half-circle is not specified.
For its filled circular region use \(0\le\theta\le\pi\), \(0\le r\le2a\sin\theta\). Then \(I=\int_0^\pi[r^3\sin\theta/3]_0^{2a\sin\theta}d\theta=(8a^3/3)\int_0^\pi\sin^4\theta d\theta\).
Using \(\int_0^\pi\sin^4\theta d\theta=3\pi/8\), this interpretation gives \(I=\pi a^3\). The printed target scales as a², while the stated integral scales as a³; it cannot hold for arbitrary a.
questions.final_answer: For the filled circle: \(\pi a^3\), not the printed \(2a^2/3\). If a different semicircular region was intended, its missing boundary must be specified.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∬r⁴sin³θ drdθ inside r=2 cosθ.
paragraphs: The whole circle is traced by \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2\), \(0\le r\le2\cos\theta\).

Radial integration gives \(I=(32/5)\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^3\theta\cos^5\theta\,d\theta\). The integrand is odd in θ and the interval is symmetric, so the integral is zero. This sign cancellation is appropriate: the printed integrand is signed, not an area.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∬r sinθ drdθ inside r=a(1−cosθ), above the initial line.
paragraphs: Assume a>0. Above the initial line, \(0\le\theta\le\pi\) and \(0\le r\le a(1-\cos\theta)\).
Put u=1−cos θ, du=sin θ dθ; u runs from 0 to 2. Then \(I=(a^2/2)\int_0^2u^2du=4a^2/3\).

question_paragraphs: Find the area bounded between r=2 cosθ and r=4 sinθ.
paragraphs: Source ambiguity: “between” two overlapping circles does not identify whether the common lens or the regions belonging to exactly one circle are wanted. Both interpretations are reported.

The circles have centres (1,0),(0,2) and radii1,2. Their nonzero intersection direction satisfies \(2\cos\alpha=4\sin\alpha\), so \(\alpha=\arctan(1/2)\). For the common lens the smaller radius is 4sin θ on [0,α], and2cos θ on [α,π/2].

\(A_{\rm common}=\dfrac12\int_0^\alpha16\sin^2\theta\,d\theta+\dfrac12\int_\alpha^{\pi/2}4\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\). Using sin2α=4/5, the first contribution is \(4\alpha-8/5\), the second \(\pi/2-\alpha-2/5\).
Hence \(A_{\rm common}=\pi/2+3\alpha-2\). The individual areas sum to5π, so the symmetric-difference area is \(5\pi-2A_{\rm common}=4\pi-6\alpha+4\).
questions.final_answer: Common lens: \(\pi/2+3\arctan(1/2)-2\). Inside exactly one circle: \(4\pi-6\arctan(1/2)+4\). The source must specify which region is intended.

question_paragraphs: Find area common to r=a(1+cosθ) and r=a(1−cosθ).
paragraphs: For a>0, intersections away from the common cusp satisfy cos θ=0. The common region has four equal contributions. On \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\), the smaller radius is a(1−cos θ).
The three integrals are π/2, 1 and π/4 respectively. Thus \(A=2a^2(3\pi/4-2)=a^2(3\pi/2-4)\).

question_paragraphs: Find area inside r=a sinθ and outside r=a(1−cosθ).
paragraphs: Assume a>0. The circle is above the initial line. Its radius exceeds the cardioid radius exactly when \(\sin\theta\ge1-\cos\theta\), which on [0,π] holds on [0,π/2].
Expand the bracket as \(-\cos2\theta-1+2\cos\theta\). Its integral is \(2-\pi/2\); hence \(A=a^2(1-\pi/4)\).

question_paragraphs: Find area of the crescent bounded by r=√3 and r=2 cosθ.
paragraphs: The two circles overlap. Interpret “crescent” as the part inside r=2cos θ but outside the circle r=√3. The other crescent is a different region, so its area is also stated.
The intersection angles satisfy2cos θ=√3, giving θ=±π/6. Thus \(A=\dfrac12\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}(4\cos^2\theta-3)d\theta=[-\theta/2+\sin2\theta/2]_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}=\sqrt3/2-\pi/6\).
The centred circle has area3π and the offset circle has areaπ. The opposite crescent (inside the centred circle, outside the offset circle) therefore has area \(2\pi+A\).
questions.final_answer: Inside r=2cos θ and outside r=√3: \(\sqrt3/2-\pi/6\). The opposite crescent has area \(11\pi/6+\sqrt3/2\).

question_paragraphs: Find area inside r=a(1+cosθ) and outside r=a.
paragraphs: For a>0 the cardioid is outside r=a precisely when cos θ≥0, i.e. \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2\).
The cosine integral is2 and the squared-cosine integral is π/2. Thus \(A=(a^2/2)(4+\pi/2)=a^2(2+\pi/4)\).

question_paragraphs: Find area inside r=3a cosθ and outside r=a(1+cosθ).
paragraphs: Assume a>0. The radial interval exists when \(3\cos\theta\ge1+\cos\theta\), so \(|\theta|\le\pi/3\).
The bracket has primitive \(3\theta+2\sin2\theta-2\sin\theta\). At the two endpoints the sine contributions cancel, leaving2π; hence A=πa².

question_paragraphs: Find whole area of r²=a²cos2θ.
paragraphs: For a>0, one loop occupies \(-\pi/4\le\theta\le\pi/4\), \(0\le r\le a\sqrt{\cos2\theta}\). There are two equal loops.

question_paragraphs: Use double integration to find area of r=a(1−cosθ).
paragraphs: Assume a>0. The full cardioid is swept once over \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). Its filled-region area is the double integral of r dr dθ.
The three terms integrate to2π,0,π. Therefore \(A=3\pi a^2/2\).

question_paragraphs: Use double integration to find area of r=a(1+cosθ).
paragraphs: Assume a>0. The full cardioid is swept once over \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). Its filled-region area is the double integral of r dr dθ.
The three terms integrate to2π,0,π. Therefore \(A=3\pi a^2/2\).

question_paragraphs: Calculate ∬r³ drdθ between r=2 sinθ and r=4 sinθ (repeated).
paragraphs: This repeats Polar integrals Q1. Keep the printed weight r³ and the printed measure drdθ.

groups.title: Change of variables: Cartesian to polar

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∫₀∞∫₀∞e^(−x²−y²) dxdy; deduce ∫₀∞e^(−x²)dx=√π/2.
paragraphs: The nonnegative integrand permits separation and polar substitution. Let \(I=\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}dx>0\). Then the double integral is I².
With x=r cos θ,y=r sin θ and Jacobian r, \(I^2=\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta\). The radial primitive is \(-e^{-r^2}/2\), so the radial integral is1/2.
Therefore \(I^2=(\pi/2)(1/2)=\pi/4\); take the positive square root to obtain \(I=\sqrt\pi/2\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^a\int_y^a\dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dx\,dy\) in polar coordinates.
paragraphs: For a>0 the region is0≤y≤x≤a. In polar coordinates \(0\le\theta\le\pi/4\), \(0\le r\le a\sec\theta\), and dxdy=r drdθ.
The integrand x/(x²+y²) times the Jacobian becomes cos θ. Hence \(I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\int_0^{a\sec\theta}\cos\theta\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/4}a\,d\theta=a\pi/4\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^{2a}\int_0^{\sqrt{2ax-x^2}}x^2\,dy\,dx\) in polar coordinates.
paragraphs: For a>0 the region is the upper half of \((x-a)^2+y^2\le a^2\). Polar coordinates give \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\), \(0\le r\le2a\cos\theta\).
Because x²=r²cos²θ and dxdy=r drdθ, \(I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2a\cos\theta}r^3\cos^2\theta\,dr\,d\theta=4a^4\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^6\theta d\theta\).
The reduction formula yields \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^6\theta d\theta=(5/6)(3/4)(1/2)(\pi/2)=5\pi/32\). Thus I=5πa⁴/8.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^2\int_0^{\sqrt{2x-x^2}}\dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy\,dx\) in polar coordinates.
paragraphs: The region is the upper half of \((x-1)^2+y^2\le1\), giving \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\), \(0\le r\le2\cos\theta\).

The rational integrand times Jacobian r is cos θ. Thus \(I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}\cos\theta drd\theta=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta d\theta=\pi/2\). The isolated origin singularity is integrable under these transformed limits.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∬(1+x²+y²)^(−3/2) dxdy over the whole plane.
paragraphs: \(I=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\dfrac{r}{(1+r^2)^{3/2}}drd\theta\). The radial primitive is \(-(1+r^2)^{-1/2}\), whose endpoint difference is1.
The angular integral is therefore \(\int_0^{2\pi}1d\theta=2\pi\). The nonnegative integral converges at both r=0 and infinity.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^a\int_0^{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}y\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,dx\,dy\) in polar coordinates.
paragraphs: Source issue: the printed differential order is dxdy, but the inner upper bound depends on x. The following answer explicitly uses the intended dy dx order over the first-quadrant quarter disk. Assume a>0.
With \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\), \(0\le r\le a\), the integrand y√(x²+y²) times Jacobian r becomes r³sin θ.
questions.final_answer: For the labelled dy dx quarter-disk interpretation: \(a^4/4\). The literal printed dependent-bound/differential combination needs correction.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∬x²y²/(x²+y²) dxdy between circles of radii a,b, b>a>0.
paragraphs: Use the annulus \(a\le r\le b\), \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\), with b>a>0. The integrand is r²cos²θsin²θ, and the Jacobian adds one factor r.

\(I=\left(\int_a^b r^3dr\right)\left(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta d\theta\right)\). The radial factor is (b⁴−a⁴)/4, while \(\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta=(1-\cos4\theta)/8\) gives angular factor π/4.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate the printed \(\int_0^a\int_0^x\int_0^{1-x-y}\dfrac1{(x+y+z)^3}\,dx\,dy\,dz\).
paragraphs: Source issue: the printed dx dy dz order is incompatible with its x- and y-dependent bounds. For a>0, even the natural intended dz dy dx order has a nonintegrable positive singularity at the origin.
Choose \(0<\epsilon<\min(a,1/3)\). Inside \(0<x<\epsilon,0<y<x,0<z<x\), all intended limits hold because \(x+y+z<3\epsilon<1\). There \((x+y+z)^{-3}\ge(3x)^{-3}\).

The y,z cross-section has area x², so this part alone contributes at least \(\int_0^\epsilon x^2/(27x^3)dx=(1/27)\int_0^\epsilon dx/x=+\infty\). A proposed order correction cannot produce a finite positive-region integral.
questions.final_answer: The printed iterated integral is not well-defined as written; the natural intended nonnegative-region integral diverges to +∞ for a>0.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭(xy+yz+zx) dxdydz over 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2,0≤z≤3.
paragraphs: The box limits are0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2,0≤z≤3. Linearity allows the three monomials to be integrated separately.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^1\int_0^x\int_0^{x+y}e^{x+y+z}\,dz\,dy\,dx\).
Evaluate ∭xyz dxdydz over the positive octant of x²+y²+z²≤a².
paragraphs: Assume a>0. Use \(x=\rho\sin\theta\cos\phi,y=\rho\sin\theta\sin\phi,z=\rho\cos\theta\), with \(0\le\rho\le a\), \(0\le\theta,\phi\le\pi/2\). The volume Jacobian is ρ²sin θ.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\iiint\dfrac{dx\,dy\,dz}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2-y^2-z^2}}\) inside the sphere of radius a.
paragraphs: Assume a>0. Spherical coordinates over the whole ball give \(I=4\pi\int_0^a\rho^2/\sqrt{a^2-\rho^2}\,d\rho\). The boundary singularity is of inverse-square-root type and is integrable.
Put ρ=a sin u,0≤u≤π/2. Since dρ=a cos u du, the radial integral becomes \(a^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2u du=\pi a^2/4\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭1 dxdydz in the tetrahedron x,y,z≥0,2x+3y+4z≤12.
paragraphs: The plane intercepts are x=6,y=4,z=3. Explicit limits are \(0\le x\le6\), \(0\le y\le4-2x/3\), \(0\le z\le3-x/2-3y/4\).
The z-integral is \(3-x/2-3y/4\). Let L=4−2x/3; because3−x/2=3L/4, the y-integral is \(3L^2/8=(6-x)^2/6\).
\(I=\int_0^6(6-x)^2/6\,dx=12\). This agrees with the tetrahedron formula6·4·3/6.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭xyz dxdydz bounded by x=0,y=0,z=1 and x²+y²=1 using cylindrical coordinates.
paragraphs: Source issue: the listed surfaces x=0,y=0,z=1 and x²+y²=1 do not provide a lower z-bound. They therefore do not specify a finite closed solid. The coordinate planes also leave the quadrant choice implicit.

If the intended solid is the first-octant quarter cylinder with the additional plane z=0, use \(0\le r\le1\), \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\), \(0\le z\le1\). Then xyz dV becomes \(r^3z\cos\theta\sin\theta\,dz\,dr\,d\theta\).
The three factors are \(\int_0^1z dz=1/2\), \(\int_0^1r^3dr=1/4\), and \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\sin\theta d\theta=1/2\). Their product is1/16.
questions.final_answer: Underdefined as printed. With the explicitly added first-octant 0≤z≤1 interpretation, the value is1/16.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭(1+x+y+z)^(−3) dxdydz in x,y,z≥0,x+y+z≤1.
paragraphs: The region is x,y,z≥0,x+y+z≤1. Put t=x+y+z, x=tu,y=tv,z=t(1−u−v). Then 0≤t≤1, u,v≥0,u+v≤1, and the Jacobian magnitude is t². The u,v triangle has area1/2.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭(x+y+z) dxdydz in x,y,z≥0,x+y+z≤1.
paragraphs: The solid is the unit simplex x,y,z≥0,x+y+z≤1. By symmetry the x,y,z first moments are equal.
For a fixed x, the y,z cross-section is a triangle of area (1−x)²/2. Hence \(\iiint x\,dV=\dfrac12\int_0^1x(1-x)^2dx=\dfrac12(1/2-2/3+1/4)=1/24\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate the printed \(\int_0^1\int_0^{1-x}\int_0^{1-x-y}\dfrac1{(1+x+y+z)^3}\,dx\,dy\,dz\).
paragraphs: Source issue: Q10 prints dx dy dz with bounds requiring dz dy dx. The following evaluates that explicitly labelled intended order.
The region is x,y,z≥0,x+y+z≤1. Put t=x+y+z, x=tu,y=tv,z=t(1−u−v). Then 0≤t≤1, u,v≥0,u+v≤1, and the Jacobian magnitude is t². The u,v triangle has area1/2.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^1\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}}xyz\,dz\,dy\,dx\).
paragraphs: The limits describe the positive octant of the unit ball. Integrate z: \(\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}}xyz\,dz=xy(1-x^2-y^2)/2\).
Let A=1−x². The y-integral from0 to√A is \(\dfrac x2\int_0^{\sqrt A}(Ay-y^3)dy=xA^2/8\).
The remaining integral is \(\dfrac18\int_0^1x(1-x^2)^2dx=\dfrac1{16}\int_0^1u^2du=1/48\), using u=1−x² and reversing endpoints.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭(x+y+z) dxdydz in the tetrahedron x,y,z≥0,x+y+z≤1 (repeated).
paragraphs: The solid is the unit simplex x,y,z≥0,x+y+z≤1. By symmetry the x,y,z first moments are equal.
For a fixed x, the y,z cross-section is a triangle of area (1−x)²/2. Hence \(\iiint x\,dV=\dfrac12\int_0^1x(1-x)^2dx=\dfrac12(1/2-2/3+1/4)=1/24\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_1^e\int_1^{\log y}\int_1^{e^x}\log z\,dz\,dx\,dy\).
paragraphs: The literal limits have 1≤y≤e and 1≥log y≥0, so the middle x-integral runs from1 down to log y. Retain this orientation; do not silently swap its limits.
\(\int_1^{e^x}\log z\,dz=[z\log z-z]_1^{e^x}=e^x(x-1)+1\). A primitive in x is \(e^x(x-2)+x\).
At x=log y and1, its difference is \(y\log y-2y+\log y+e-1\). Integrate y from1 to e using \(\int y\log y\,dy=(y^2/2)\log y-y^2/4\) and \(\int\log y\,dy=y\log y-y\).
The result is \(e^2/4-2e+13/4\), approximately−0.339299632. Its negative sign is consistent with reversed x-limits and a nonnegative inner z-integral.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty\dfrac{dx\,dy\,dz}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^2}\).
paragraphs: In the positive octant use \(0\le\theta,\phi\le\pi/2\), \(0<\rho<\infty\). The integrand is ρ⁻⁴ and the volume Jacobian is ρ²sin θ.

The angular factor is \((\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin\theta d\theta)(\int_0^{\pi/2}d\phi)=\pi/2\). The remaining radial integral is \(\int_0^\infty\rho^{-2}d\rho\), whose lower-end integral \(\int_\epsilon^1\rho^{-2}d\rho=1/\epsilon-1\) tends to∞.
The finite tail from1 to∞ cannot cancel this nonnegative origin divergence.

question_paragraphs: Find volume bounded by coordinate planes and x/a+y/b+z/c=1.
paragraphs: Assume a,b,c>0, as positive coordinate intercepts. Scale x=au,y=bv,z=cw. The Jacobian magnitude is abc and the new region is u,v,w≥0,u+v+w≤1.

question_paragraphs: Use a triple integral to find volume inside x²/a²+y²/b²+z²/c²=1.
paragraphs: Assume a,b,c>0. Scale x=au,y=bv,z=cw, so the ellipsoid becomes u²+v²+w²≤1 and the Jacobian is abc.
The three factors are1/3,2,2π. Thus \(V=4\pi abc/3\).

question_paragraphs: Find volume bounded by x=0,y=0,z=0,x+y+z=a.
paragraphs: Assume a>0. The bounded first-octant tetrahedron has limits \(0\le x\le a\), \(0\le y\le a-x\), \(0\le z\le a-x-y\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭1 in x,y,z≥0,2x+3y+4z≤12 (repeated).
paragraphs: This repeats Triple integrals Q6. The intercepts are6,4,3, and the explicit volume integral is \(\int_0^6\int_0^{4-2x/3}\int_0^{3-x/2-3y/4}dz\,dy\,dx\).
The z- and y-integrals reduce it to \(\int_0^6(6-x)^2/6\,dx=12\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate \(\int_0^1\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx\) in spherical coordinates.
paragraphs: The denominator is √(1−x²−y²), with no z² term. The region is the positive octant of the unit ball. In spherical coordinates \(0\le\rho\le1\), \(0\le\theta,\phi\le\pi/2\).

The transformed integral is \(I=\dfrac\pi2\int_0^1\rho^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2\sin^2\theta}}d\theta\,d\rho\). Set v=cos θ to evaluate the inner integral as \(\operatorname{atanh}(\rho)/\rho\) for0<ρ<1.
Thus \(I=(\pi/2)\int_0^1\rho\operatorname{atanh}\rho\,d\rho\). A primitive is \(\rho/2+(\rho^2-1)\operatorname{atanh}\rho/2\); its endpoint values are0 and1/2 (by the limit at1). Hence I=π/4.
Independent check: integrating z first cancels the original denominator, leaving the area π/4 of the quarter unit disk.
questions.final_answer: \(\pi/4\). Directly, integrating z cancels the denominator and leaves the quarter-unit-disk area.

question_paragraphs: Use cylindrical coordinates to find volume of a cylinder of radius a,height h.
paragraphs: Assume a,h>0. A cylinder with its axis along z has limits \(0\le r\le a\), \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\), \(0\le z\le h\). The cylindrical Jacobian is r.

question_paragraphs: Transform \(\int_0^1\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\int_{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}^1\dfrac{dx\,dy\,dz}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}\) to spherical coordinates and evaluate.
paragraphs: Source issue: the printed differentials dx dy dz conflict with the displayed x- and y-dependent bounds. Under the explicitly intended dz dy dx order, the region is x,y≥0 and √(x²+y²)≤z≤1. It is the first-quadrant cone capped by z=1.

In spherical coordinates z≥√(x²+y²) means \(0\le\theta\le\pi/4\); z≤1 means \(0\le\rho\le\sec\theta\); and \(0\le\phi\le\pi/2\). The original quarter-disk radial bound is automatic from these cone/cap inequalities.

The integrand1/ρ times Jacobianρ²sin θ isρsin θ. Therefore \(I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\sec\theta}\rho\sin\theta\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi=\dfrac\pi4\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin\theta\sec^2\theta d\theta\).
The remaining primitive is sec θ, giving \(I=\pi(\sqrt2-1)/4\) under that labelled order correction.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭(x²+y²+z²) in the unit ball using spherical coordinates.
paragraphs: Over the whole unit ball use \(0\le\rho\le1,0\le\theta\le\pi,0\le\phi\le2\pi\). Since x²+y²+z²=ρ², multiplying by the volume Jacobian givesρ⁴sin θ.

question_paragraphs: Find sphere volume x²+y²+z²≤a² by triple integration.
paragraphs: For a>0, integrate the spherical Jacobian over \(0\le\rho\le a,0\le\theta\le\pi,0\le\phi\le2\pi\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭1/(x²+y²+z²) inside the sphere of radius a.
paragraphs: For a>0, use the whole-ball spherical limits. The reciprocal-radius-squared integrand ρ⁻² cancels the factorρ² in the Jacobian.
\(I=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^a\sin\theta d\rho d\theta d\phi=a(2)(2\pi)=4\pi a\). The singularity atρ=0 is integrable because the remaining radial integrand is constant.

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭(x+y+z) over the first octant of the ball radius a.
paragraphs: For a>0, first-octant limits are \(0\le\rho\le a,0\le\theta,\phi\le\pi/2\). Substitute \(x+y+z=\rho[\sin\theta(\cos\phi+\sin\phi)+\cos\theta]\) and dV=ρ²sin θ dρdθdφ.

The radial integral gives a⁴/4. For the angular factor, \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2\theta d\theta=\pi/4\), \(\int_0^{\pi/2}(\cos\phi+\sin\phi)d\phi=2\), \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin\theta\cos\theta d\theta=1/2\), and the φ-length isπ/2.
Thus the angular factor is \((\pi/4)(2)+(1/2)(\pi/2)=3\pi/4\). Multiply by a⁴/4 to obtain \(3\pi a^4/16\).

question_paragraphs: Evaluate ∭1/√(x²+y²+z²) between spheres of radii a>b>0.
paragraphs: For a>b>0, the shell has \(b\le\rho\le a,0\le\theta\le\pi,0\le\phi\le2\pi\). The reciprocal-radius integrand times the volume Jacobian isρsin θ.
